title: Memory stitching and backing-store spill strategy for KV residency (draft)
summary: This is an exploratory design note for a "memory stitching" approach to managing KV cache residency across GPU local memory and host backing stores (NUMA/UMA and NVMe/PCIe-attached memory). The goal is to provide a low-latency, resilient spill mechanism that preserves token-level SLOs by combining fine-grained residency metadata, opportunistic stitching of KV blocks from multiple sources, and a priority-aware eviction/prefetch policy. This doc is intentionally high-level with concrete heuristics and an experiment plan to validate tradeoffs.
motivation:
- Current serving workloads see a bimodal pattern: short interactive sessions with tight latency budgets and long-batched churn for high-throughput inference. A one-size-fits-all offload policy either hurts latency or wastes host RAM/GPU memory.
- PCIe-attached NVMe and remote memory (UMA-like host regions) are useful backing stores but have wildly different latency and throughput characteristics and different failure modes (IO stalls, driver interrupts, thermal throttling).
- We need an approach that can keep the hot subset resident on GPU while maintaining correctness/performance when colder KV frames are stitched together from multiple backing layers without incurring full re-materialization costs.
constraints & non-goals:
- This doc assumes the runtime already supports per-request KV addressing and a small per-token async prefetch API. It does not redesign attention/cache formats.
- Not proposing changes to customer-facing APIs. All changes are internal to the runtime and deployment configs.
- Target SLOs: p50 < 20ms for interactive paths, p95 < 100ms in steady-state; but design should gracefully trade latency for throughput in dedicated tiers.
key ideas:
1) Memory stitching: represent a logical KV frame as ordered microblocks. When a request needs values, the runtime can stitch microblocks sourced from GPU L2, host DRAM pages, or NVMe segments into a temporary in-GPU fast-path buffer. Stitching is cheap compared to full rehydrate if microblocks are sized for cacheline-friendly GPU DMA operations.
2) Residency classes: classify microblocks into HOT / WARM / COLD / GUARDED.
   - HOT: pinned in GPU memory; immediate access.
   - WARM: resident in host NUMA local DRAM (low-latency UMA region) and eligible for async DMA into GPU.
   - COLD: only on persistent NVMe or remote host regions; fetch cost is higher, prefetch/gentle throttles apply.
   - GUARDED: eviction-protected region for recent canaries or policy-marked keys (e.g., high-priority customer).
3) Priority-aware eviction: when reclaiming GPU memory, evict microblocks grouped by score = access_frequency * recency_weight * customer_priority. Eviction decisions prefer demoting to WARM (host DRAM) instead of moving straight to NVMe when possible.
4) PCIe-aware IO capping: maintain moving-window metrics (PCIe tail latency, in-flight transfers, NVMe queue depth). When PCIe tail exceeds threshold, down-prioritize background prefetch and switch to on-demand stitching with degraded SLO targets.
5) Opportunistic prefetching: prefetch WARM candidates into a small, rotating pinned buffer during low PCIe load. Prefetch policy uses request-level hints (future seq length predictions) and model-driven scoring.
6) Stitch cache: a short-lived transient stitched-buffer cache on GPU for microblocks that were stitched recently; avoids repeated DMA for repeated near-term accesses.
implementation sketch:
- Residency metadata store: per-model vector of microblock entries: {microblock_id, size, checksum, residency_class, last_access_ts, score}. Keep compact and cache on-GPU for hot indices.
- Microblock size: aim for 8KB-64KB range. Rationale: fits DMA granularity on modern GPUs and avoids excessive CPU/GPU overhead. Tunable by model class.
- DMA engine: reuse existing async copy primitives. Support scatter-gather fetch where multiple microblocks are combined into one pinned GPU buffer prior to attention execution.
- IO scheduler shim: user-space controller that monitors kernel NVMe stats (latency percentiles, dma throughput) and kernel memory pressure. It applies backpressure to prefetch queues and exposes fast-path boolean to the request executor: allow_stitch_prefetch.
- Fallbacks: if a stitched fetch misses (NVMe read too slow or fails), runtime should have a bounded retry/leap strategy: 1) try alternate host NUMA region, 2) do-on-demand re-compute from weights (if available) or run a degraded small-model fallback. Prefer graceful degradation.
threshold heuristics (initial picks to t:
- GPU eviction watermark: free GPU memory < 10% triggers eviction events.
- Demote-to-WARM threshold: predicted reuse_window > 100ms -> demote to host DRAM instead of NVMe.
- PCIe tail threshold: 95th percentile DMA latency > 3ms -> pause non-critical prefetches.
- Stitch buffer size: 4MB per model shard, rotating LRU.
- Max concurrent NVMe fetches per GPU: 16 (subject to tuning by profiling).
metrics to collect (essential for decidi:
- per-microblock access histogram (counts & inter-arrival times)
- PCIe/NVMe p50/p95/p99 DMA latency per workload
- number of stitched buffers reused vs cold stitched
- eviction rates and where demoted blocks land (host DRAM vs NVMe)
- request-level latency deltas when a stitch occurs vs hot-resident path
- tail SLO violations correlated with NVMe activity spikes
experiments & rollout plan:
1) lab-only microbench: synthetic trace generator with hot/cold key distributions and configured PCIe latency injectors. Validate microblock size and DMA batching strategy.
2) Canary on Dedicated: enable memory-stitching in canary pool with conservative PCIe thresholds, collect metrics and tune thresholds for prod-like models.
3) Progressive exposure: allow product teams to opt into GUARD region tagging for critical customers; measure difference.
4) Full default offload: after 3 weeks + SLO review, flip offload to go-live on dedicated non-sensitive fleets.
operational considerations:
- Observability: surface a "residency map" for models in Console with heatmap tiles, eviction events, and PCIe saturation alerts.
- Cost accounting: track extra PCIe/NVMe egress and attribute to tenant to inform price/commit sizing.
- Safety knobs: global and per-customer throttles; emergency disable for prefetch.
open questions / risks:
- NUMA locality: in multi-socket hosts, moving blocks to host DRAM in wrong NUMA node can worsen latency. Do we bind WARM regions to GPU-preferred NUMA nodes? Requires host placement policy integration.
- Checksum & corruption handling: stitching mixes blocks from different stores; need end-to-end checksums and fast invalidation path.
- Fallback complexity: re-materialization from weights is powerful but expensive; do we want a tiered fallback (small-model hallucination vs degrade accuracy)?
- Driver/kernel visibility: not all metrics may be available in user-space on all distros; consider a small eBPF probe for tail latencies.
next steps (short-term):
- Prototype microblock metadata and stitching buffer in an internal branch (runtime/stitching-proto).
- Build synthetic trace generator and PCIe latency injection harness.
- Create dashboard panels: "stitched fetch rate", "stitch latency", "eviction landing distribution".
notes:
- This doc deliberately focuses on the middle layer (runtime + user-space IO controller). Kernel-level page-fault handler tuning should be captured in a separate ops runbook.
- We expect the final production variant to expose only a small set of tunables (watermarks, max concurrent fetches, guarded list), keeping the default conservative.
